title: Moving Average from Data Stream
description: Brute force to optimized: rescanning the window every call versus a queue with a running sum updated incrementally.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Given a stream of integers and a window size, calculate the moving average of all integers in the sliding window. Implement the MovingAverage class: MovingAverage(int size) initializes the object with the window size; double next(int val) adds val to the stream and returns the moving average of the LAST size values (or fewer, if fewer than size values have arrived so far).

blocks.caption: A queue holding exactly the last "size" values, alongside a running sum, directly computes each moving average in O(1)

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","A window size, and a sequence of calls to next(val)"],["Output","For each call, the average of the last (up to) size values seen"],["Goal","Answer each call in O(1), rather than recomputing the average from scratch each time"],["Constraints","1 <= size <= 1000; -10^5 <= val <= 10^5; at most 10^4 calls to next"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["A FIXED-SIZE sliding window of the MOST RECENT values","A queue directly models this: new values enqueue at the back, and the oldest value is evicted from the front once the window exceeds its size"],["The average changes incrementally with each new value","Maintaining a running SUM (updated by simple addition/subtraction) avoids ever needing to rescan the window to recompute it"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

At any point, only the LAST "size" values (or fewer, if the stream is still shorter than the window) matter for the average; as new values arrive, the OLDEST value in the current window must be dropped once the window would otherwise grow beyond its fixed size.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Rolling GPA Calculated From Only Your Most Recent Courses
blocks.text: Imagine calculating a rolling grade-point-average using only your most recent N courses: as a new grade comes in, it joins the average, and if you now have more than N grades on record, the OLDEST one drops off entirely, no longer counted. A queue directly tracks exactly this "most recent N" set, and keeping a running total (rather than re-adding every grade each time) makes updating the average instant.

blocks.caption: Each new value enqueues and adds to the running sum; once the queue exceeds the window size, the oldest value is dequeued and subtracted back out

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: size = 3; next(1), next(10), next(3), next(5)
5. How Should We Think?

Before recomputing the sum of the current window from scratch on every single call (rescanning up to "size" values each time), notice that maintaining a running sum, updated incrementally as values enter and leave the window, makes each call O(1).

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A queue directly and naturally maintains "the most recent size values," since new values always enqueue at the back, and the window's size constraint means the OLDEST value (at the front) is exactly what must be evicted once the window overflows.

Observation 2: Rather than summing the entire queue's contents on every call, a running sum can be maintained incrementally: adding the newly enqueued value, and subtracting any value that gets evicted.

Observation 3: The average itself is then simply the running sum divided by the CURRENT queue size (which may be smaller than "size" during the initial ramp-up period, before the window has fully filled).

Observation 4: This combination (a queue for tracking membership, a running sum for the total) achieves O(1) per call, regardless of the window size.

This is the sliding-window-with-running-aggregate technique: a queue tracks exactly which values are currently "in the window," while a running sum (updated incrementally) avoids ever needing to rescan.
6. Brute Force Solution
Store every value seen so far in a list, trimming from the front if the window size is exceeded, and recompute the sum by rescanning the entire current window on every single call.
Step by step algorithm

items: Append the new value to the list; if the list now exceeds the window size, remove the oldest (front) value.
Sum every value currently in the list, and divide by the list's length, to compute the average.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Trimming from the front directly maintains the "last size values" window, though at O(n) cost per removal on a plain list.
Rescanning the entire window to compute the sum is the most direct interpretation of "average," but repeats the same summation work every single call.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
Correctly computes the moving average, since it directly sums the current window's exact contents each time.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(size) per call, for both the front removal and the resummation.
Space: O(size), for the stored window.
Limitation: resumming the entire window on every call is unnecessary; maintaining a running sum incrementally achieves the same result in O(1) per call.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force resums the window from scratch every call. Instead, maintain a queue (for tracking which values are in the window) alongside a running sum (updated incrementally): on each next(val), enqueue val and add it to the running sum; if the queue now exceeds the window size, dequeue the oldest value and subtract it from the running sum. The average is simply runningSum divided by the queue's current size.

Maintain a deque and a runningSum variable (starting at 0). On next(val): enqueue val, add val to runningSum; if the queue's size exceeds "size," dequeue the front value and subtract it from runningSum. Return runningSum divided by the queue's current size.
9. Optimized Solution
Maintain a queue and a running sum, updated incrementally on every call, avoiding any need to rescan the window.
Dry run for size = 3, next(1), next(10), next(3), next(5)

blocks.title: Final answer
blocks.text: The sequence of averages is 1, 5.5, 4.66667, 6, matching the expected results.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(1) per call, for both the queue operations and the running sum updates.
Space: O(size), for the queue holding the current window.
Why This Works

Since the running sum is updated by exactly the SAME amount that the actual window's total changes by (adding the new value, subtracting any evicted value), it always stays perfectly synchronized with the sum of whatever is currently in the queue, without ever needing to be recomputed from scratch. Dividing by the queue's CURRENT size (not always the fixed window size) correctly handles the initial ramp-up period, before the window has fully filled.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["The window has not yet filled to its full size","The queue's current (smaller) size is used as the divisor, correctly averaging over however many values have arrived so far"],["The window is full and a new value arrives","The oldest value is evicted and subtracted from the running sum, keeping the window at exactly \"size\" values"],["Every call","O(1) work: one enqueue, one sum addition, and (conditionally) one dequeue and sum subtraction"]]}

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: The running sum is updated in the SAME step as each enqueue/dequeue, never as a separate rescanning pass.
The eviction check (queue size exceeds the window size) correctly triggers only once the window would otherwise grow too large, never prematurely.
Dividing by the queue's actual current length (not a hardcoded "size") correctly handles the early calls, before the window has fully filled up.

blocks.text: 10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Time","Space","Notes"],"rows":[["Brute force (rescan and resum the window every call)","O(size) per call","O(size)","Correct, but repeats the same summation work unnecessarily"],["Optimized (queue + running sum)","O(1) per call","O(size)","Updates the sum incrementally, never rescanning the window"]]}

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

A fixed-size sliding window over a stream is a natural fit for a queue (tracking membership) paired with a running AGGREGATE (like a sum), updated incrementally as values enter and leave the window, avoiding any need to ever rescan.
Common mistakes

items: Recomputing the sum by rescanning the queue on every call, missing the O(1) incremental-update opportunity entirely.
Dividing by a fixed "size" instead of the queue's CURRENT size, which would be incorrect during the initial ramp-up period before the window fills.
Forgetting to subtract the evicted value from the running sum, leaving it silently incorrect after the first eviction.

blocks.text: Edge cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["Window size of 1","Every call's average is simply the most recent value itself"],["Fewer values have arrived than the window size","The average is correctly computed over whatever HAS arrived so far, using the queue's current (smaller) size"],["A very large number of calls (near the constraint limit)","The O(1)-per-call technique scales linearly overall, unlike the brute force's O(size) per call"]]}

blocks.text: Interview tips

items: Explicitly stating "maintain a running sum incrementally, never recompute it" demonstrates the key optimization insight clearly and directly.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Fixed-size sliding window over a STREAM, needing an aggregate like sum/average" points toward a queue for membership tracking, paired with a running aggregate updated incrementally.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would you extend this to also support a moving MAXIMUM or MINIMUM (not just average)? A running sum works for sums, but max/min require a different structure (a monotonic deque), since removing an arbitrary element from a running max/min is not simply "subtract it back out" the way sums allow.

How would you handle a window defined by TIME (not a fixed count of values), similar to Number of Recent Calls? The exact same queue-based eviction technique applies, just checking timestamps against a time threshold instead of a fixed count.

What if new values could also be REMOVED from the middle of the stream after being added? A queue alone would no longer suffice; a different structure (like an indexed balanced tree) would be needed to support arbitrary removal efficiently.

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: A direct application of the sliding-window queue pattern shared with Number of Recent Calls elsewhere in this category, here additionally maintaining a running SUM rather than just a count.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(size) per call; O(size) space.
Optimized (queue + running sum): O(1) per call; O(size) space.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: Sliding-window queue with a running aggregate (sum)
Core Idea: A queue tracks exactly the current window's membership; a running sum, updated incrementally on every enqueue/dequeue, avoids ever needing to rescan the window
Time: O(1) per call
Space: O(size)
Most Important Observation: Dividing by the queue's CURRENT size (not the fixed window size) correctly handles the initial ramp-up period before the window fully fills
Interview Difficulty: Easy
One-line memory trick: Enqueue + add to sum; if oversized, dequeue + subtract from sum; average = sum / queue size
